title: Working in the UK: A Practical Guide for African Professionals
excerpt: An honest look at the Skilled Worker and Graduate visa routes, what sponsorship really means, and the true costs and timelines African professionals should plan for.
content:
When Tunde told his colleagues in Lagos that he was moving to Manchester, nobody asked about the weather. The first question was: who is sponsoring you? That question sits at the centre of everything in this guide. The UK does not run a lottery you win with luck. It runs a rules based system, and once you understand the rules you can treat the move like any serious project: with a budget, a timeline, and a shortlist of target employers.

Below are the two main routes for professionals, a third door for health workers, the real costs, and the mistakes that quietly sink strong candidates. Every figure here comes from official UK government pages I checked at the time of writing. Rules change often, so confirm the current numbers on gov.uk before you spend a single naira, shilling or cedi.

Three doors into the UK job market

Most African professionals enter through one of three visa routes. Each has its own logic, and choosing the wrong one can cost you months.

RouteWho it fitsKey requirement
Skilled Worker visaExperienced professionals with a UK job offer in handA certificate of sponsorship from a Home Office approved employer, plus a salary that meets the threshold for the role
Graduate visaPeople willing to complete a UK degree firstAn eligible qualification finished in the UK on a Student visa; no employer sponsor needed
Health and Care Worker visaDoctors, nurses, health professionals and adult social care workersAn eligible health job with the NHS, an NHS supplier or in adult social care

The Skilled Worker route: sponsorship is everything

You cannot apply for a Skilled Worker visa and then look for work. It runs the other way. First an employer offers you a job, then that employer issues you a certificate of sponsorship, and only then do you apply. The employer must hold a sponsor licence from the Home Office, which is why the most useful document in your entire job search is free. The government publishes a register of licensed sponsors listing every organisation that can legally sponsor workers, and it is updated almost daily. Download it, filter it to your industry, and build your application list from it. A software engineer in Accra who targets fifty licensed sponsors will get further than one who sprays five hundred random job boards.

Money matters too. The standard rule is that the job must pay at least £41,700 a year or the going rate for the occupation, whichever is higher. There are genuine discounts, though. Jobs on the immigration salary list can qualify at £33,400, and if you are under 26 or a recent graduate, the new entrant rules allow 70 percent of the going rate as long as you still earn at least £33,400. Health workers get the best deal of all: a nurse from Nairobi or a care professional from Johannesburg on the Health and Care Worker route pays no health surcharge at all, which saves thousands of pounds over a five year stay.

The Graduate route: study first, then breathe

The second door is slower but more forgiving. You come on a Student visa, which costs £558 and can be applied for up to six months before your course starts. You complete your degree, then switch to a Graduate visa for £937 plus the health surcharge. That visa currently lasts two years if you apply on or before 31 December 2026, and drops to 18 months for applications from 1 January 2027. PhD graduates get three years.

Here is what makes the route powerful: no sponsor is needed. You can take almost any job, freelance, or search freely. Here is what makes it dangerous: it cannot be extended. Treat it as a runway, not a destination. Your mission from month one is to convert into a Skilled Worker visa with a licensed sponsor. The graduates who struggle are usually the ones who spend the first year settling in and only begin serious applications when the clock is nearly finished.

What it really costs

Budget honestly before you begin. For a Skilled Worker application from outside the UK, expect:

  • Application fee: £819 for a visa of up to three years, or £1,618 for longer, per person
  • Immigration health surcharge: usually £1,035 for each year of the visa, paid upfront, and waived on the Health and Care Worker route
  • Proof of funds: at least £1,270 in your bank account, unless your employer certifies your maintenance
  • Everything else: an approved English test, a tuberculosis test where your country requires one, document costs, flights, and your first month of rent plus deposit

If you bring a spouse and children, the fee and the surcharge repeat for every dependant, so a family of four should budget several multiples of the headline figure. The study route costs more again once tuition and living expenses are added, which is why so many families treat it as a long term investment rather than a quick move.

Timelines you can plan around

The application itself is the fast part. Applying from outside the UK, both the Student visa and the Skilled Worker visa usually get a decision within three weeks. The slow part is everything before that: researching sponsors, interviewing across time zones, gathering documents, and sitting your English test. Give the whole journey 6 to 12 months from first application to arrival and you will rarely be disappointed. The long game is worth understanding too. After five years on the Skilled Worker route you can usually apply for permanent settlement, which is the real prize for most families.

The mistakes that sink good candidates

Let me be blunt, because this is where dreams and savings get destroyed. Nobody legitimate sells certificates of sponsorship, so anyone in Lagos, Accra or Nairobi offering a guaranteed UK job for a fee is running a scam, and paying them can wreck your immigration record as well as your wallet. Applying to hundreds of companies that hold no sponsor licence is a slower way to lose: the register exists, so use it. People also resign from good jobs at home before any visa is granted, arrive without a cushion for the expensive first months, and send the same CV they used at home into a market with completely different expectations. And on the Graduate route, the classic error is drifting: eighteen months to two years feels long until you are six months from expiry with no sponsor in sight. None of these mistakes comes from lack of talent. They come from lack of planning, and every one of them is avoidable.

Your first moves this week

  • Download the sponsor register and build a shortlist of 30 to 50 licensed employers in your field.
  • Rebuild your CV for UK expectations before you send a single application. Our guide to writing a CV that gets interviews shows you how.
  • Start warm outreach to people already working at your target companies. Most roles are filled through relationships, as we explain in our piece on the hidden job market.
  • Compare your options honestly. If you have strong qualifications but no UK job offer, Canada's Express Entry system rewards points rather than sponsorship and may fit you better.
  • Open a dedicated savings plan for visa fees, the surcharge and your landing costs, and review it monthly.

The UK route rewards preparation over hope. Thousands of African professionals make this move every year, not because they were lucky, but because they treated it like a project. Start your list this week, and give yourself the honest timeline the move deserves.
